new_statements.quote: Contrastive word stress was noted in Ama, and possibly in Rocky Peak, Bo, and Owiniga. Examples from Ama are: [i'wa 'water' / 'iwa 'leaf'; a'mu 'moon' / 'amu 'nose'; mʌ'la 'path' / 'mʌla 'vine']. Syllable types CV, V and VV were found, with closed syllables only in Bo and consonant clusters only in Nimo and Owiniga.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Checked (ANU Open Research scan, 36 pp., text present) by rendering p. 10 (printed p. 10) and reading it visually. The passage is there, immediately below Figure C "Summary of Arai Phonology": "Contrastive word stress was noted in Ama, and possibly in Rocky Peak, Bo, and Owiniga. Examples from Ama are: i'wa water / 'iwa leaf; a'mu moon / 'amu nose; mʌ'ľa path / 'mʌľa vine. Syllable types CV, V and VV were found, with closed syllables only in Bo and consonant clusters only in Nimo and Owiniga." The only difference from the compiler quote is that the l in the Ama path/vine pair carries a caron (ľ, the l/ľ/r/ř liquid series of Figure C); the compiler had bracketed that pair as scanned-uncertai…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only published statement is a hedged survey remark: word stress is contrastive (lexically distinctive, hence not positionally predictable) in Ama and 'possibly' also in Owiniga. No placement rule, no Owiniga examples; the illustrated minimal pairs are Ama disyllables with stress on either syllable. The 2024 Uppsala sketch, based on Bible translations, says nothing about stress and leaves even tonal status open.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the claim itself is hedged ('possibly') and rests on a 102-item survey wordlist.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('word stress'), citation forms from wordlist elicitation via Tok Pisin; the Ama examples in the quote are bracketed because the vowel symbol in 'mʌla' is read from a noisy scanned of the scan (the stress marks and glosses are clear).
new_statements.identity_note: Conrad & Dye 1975 call the language 'Owiniga' and its family 'Arai' (= Left May, left1242); the Uppsala thesis and Escott use the NTM spelling 'Owininga'. All refer to the same language, owin1240 (ISO owi); no dialects are distinguished in any source seen.
